# Interpolation and Sampling Techniques

Also called: Trilinear Interpolation (DRR), Trilinear rendering

## Overview
Interpolation and Sampling Techniques define how scalar field values are reconstructed from discrete voxel samples during volume ray casting, directly influencing image quality and computational cost [S1, unofficial][S2]. This family focuses on the spatial reconstruction kernel and weight functions applied to neighboring samples, distinguishing it from sibling techniques like [Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing via Ray Distribution](1219-multi-sample-anti-aliasing-via-ray-distribution.md) which handles sample distribution, and [Depth to Distance Conversion](2428-depth-to-distance-conversion.md) which handles geometric buffers [G]. It builds on [Direct volume ray casting](19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md) by providing the mechanism for evaluating the volume function $V(\mathbf{p})$ at arbitrary ray positions.

## Shared principles
All interpolation schemes in this family map a query position $\mathbf{p}$ in voxel space to a scalar value $V(\mathbf{p})$ by combining a finite set of neighboring voxel values $V_i$ using a set of weights $w_i(\mathbf{p})$:
$$ V(\mathbf{p}) = \sum_{i} w_i(\mathbf{p}) V_i $$
The weights are derived from a reconstruction kernel $h(\mathbf{z})$, where $\mathbf{z}$ is the distance from the query point to the sample center [G]. The choice of kernel defines the trade-off between computational complexity, spatial extent (number of neighbors), and frequency response (aliasing vs. blurring) [S1, unofficial][S2].

## Subtopics

### [Interpolation Schemes for Volume Rendering](817-interpolation-schemes-for-volume-rendering.md)
Interpolation schemes determine how scalar field values are reconstructed from discrete voxel samples during volume ray casting, directly influencing image quality and computational cost. This family focuses on the spatial reconstruction kernel and weight functions applied to neighboring samples, distinguishing it from sibling techniques like [Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing via Ray Distribution](1219-multi-sample-anti-aliasing-via-ray-distribution.md) which handles sample distribution, and [Depth to Distance Conversion](2428-depth-to-distance-conversion.md) which handles geometric buffers [G].

### [Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing via Ray Distribution](1219-multi-sample-anti-aliasing-via-ray-distribution.md)
Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing (MSAA) via Ray Distribution reduces jagged edges in volume rendering by casting multiple rays per pixel, distributed within the pixel area, and averaging the results. Unlike single-ray casting, which suffers from aliasing artifacts at silhouette edges due to coarse per-pixel sampling granularity, this method samples the scene at a higher effective resolution. It is distinct from [Supersampling](3493-supersampling.md) in its specific implementation of fixed offset patterns derived from fragment coordinates, and from [Epipolar Sampling](3899-epipolar-sampling.md) which exploits geometric constraints along epipolar lines.

### [Depth to Distance Conversion](2428-depth-to-distance-conversion.md)
Depth to Distance Conversion transforms sampled depth values ($z_{vals}$) along a ray into segment lengths ($dists$) required for volume rendering integration. It accounts for the viewing angle by scaling the depth differences with the cosine of the angle between the ray direction and the viewing direction. This method is distinct from [Interpolation Schemes for Volume Rendering](817-interpolation-schemes-for-volume-rendering.md) as it focuses on metric length calculation rather than value estimation, and from [Sampling and Jittering](2516-sampling-and-jittering.md) as it operates on already sampled points.

### [Alpha Grid Mask](2430-alpha-grid-mask.md)
Alpha Grid Mask is a module for sampling alpha (opacity) values from a precomputed 3D alpha volume using trilinear interpolation. It solves the problem of incorporating spatially varying opacity constraints into volume rendering pipelines by mapping raw mask values to a specified opacity range, preventing complete occlusion or invisibility artifacts. It differs from direct intensity sampling by applying a linear remapping to ensure sampled values fall within a valid $[min\_opacity, max\_opacity]$ interval.

### [Sampling and Jittering](2516-sampling-and-jittering.md)

### [Supersampling](3493-supersampling.md)
Supersampling is a technique to minimize aliasing artifacts by casting multiple rays per pixel and averaging the results, effectively sampling the scene at a higher spatial frequency than the displayed resolution. It sets itself apart from its siblings by uniformly increasing sample density across the pixel area (or slab depth) to combat the coarse granularity of per-pixel sampling, whereas [Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing via Ray Distribution](1219-multi-sample-anti-aliasing-via-ray-distribution.md) focuses on specific ray distribution patterns and [Adaptive Supersampling] (not a sibling article, but a variant discussed in sources) targets high-contrast areas. It builds on [Interpolation and Sampling Techniques](2787-interpolation-and-sampling-techniques.md) by defining sample points at a higher frequency than voxel spacing.

### [Epipolar Sampling](3899-epipolar-sampling.md)
Epipolar Sampling is a technique to sample features from other views along epipolar lines for a given ray, enabling cross-view feature aggregation without full 3D volume rendering during the encoding phase. It differs from standard volume rendering by operating in 2D image space using epipolar geometry to align features from source views to a target view, rather than integrating density along 3D rays in world space.

### [Voronoi-Based Foveated Volume Rendering](6463-voronoi-based-foveated-volume-rendering.md)
Voronoi-Based Foveated Volume Rendering is a method that accelerates direct volume ray casting by adapting sampling density and reconstruction quality to the human visual acuity fall-off, using gaze tracking to shift a pre-computed sampling mask and reconstructing via Voronoi-based natural neighbor interpolation. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Supersampling](3493-supersampling.md) and [Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing via Ray Distribution](1219-multi-sample-anti-aliasing-via-ray-distribution.md) by explicitly modeling the non-uniform resolution of the human eye to reduce computational cost in the periphery, while using [Temporal Smoothing for Foveated Rendering](6465-temporal-smoothing-for-foveated-rendering.md) to mitigate the specific undersampling artifacts inherent to sparse peripheral sampling.

### Slab-based Ray Sampling
In slab-based ray sampling, each slab of thickness $2d$ is defined by three successive samples ($s_f, s_m, s_b$). The next slab is indexed by $(s_f, s_m, s_b)$ with the correlation $s_f = s_b$, meaning the front sample of the next slab equals the back sample of the current slab [S2]. After retrieving the scalar values for $s_f, s_m, s_b$ from the 3D volume, the color and opacity values are given by a 3D texture-dependent fetch in the 3D pre-integration table [S2]. A front-to-back compositing algorithm then blends the successive slabs to obtain the final pixel color [S2].

### Space Warping (Log+Warp)
Space Warping warps 3D space towards the view cell center using radial distortion to bring the background closer for positional encoding, dampening high frequencies in the background while preserving foreground detail [S3]. The warping function is defined as:
$$ W(\mathbf{p}) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{|\mathbf{p}| \cdot d_{max}}} $$
where $\mathbf{p}$ is the position relative to the view cell center [S3]. The warped feature vector is computed as:
$$ \mathbf{f} = \text{encode}((\mathbf{x}(\tilde{d}_i) - \mathbf{c}) \cdot W(\mathbf{x}(\tilde{d}_i) - \mathbf{c})) $$
where $\tilde{d}_i$ is the logarithmic depth [S3]. While ray samples do not follow a straight line after warping, sample locations in space stay consistent, i.e., samples from different view points landing at the same 3D location are evaluated equally [S3].

### Space-covering volume sampling
Space-covering volume sampling is a technique proposed to extend pre-integrated volume rendering to multidimensional transfer functions [S4]. It addresses the limitation of standard pre-integration which typically relies on piecewise linear segments, by using a space-covering approach to better approximate the integral in multidimensional transfer function spaces [S4].

## Background
Trilinear interpolation is widely used in volume rendering for generating Digital Radiographic Reconstructions (DRR) due to its speed advantage over exact intersection methods like Siddon's method [S1, unofficial]. Siddon's method computes exact intersections of every cast ray with voxels, taking approximately 25 ms for a standard view, while trilinear interpolation can render the same view in ~737 μs with 25 sample points [S1, unofficial]. The rendering cost of trilinear interpolation matches Siddon's method when the number of points ($n_{points}$) is about 2,000 [S1, unofficial]. Performance scales linearly with $n_{points}$: 50 points take ~1.03 ms, 100 points take ~1.65 ms, and 5,000 points take ~66 ms [S1, unofficial].

Space warping techniques were introduced in the context of neural radiance fields (NeRF) to handle the disparity between foreground and background frequency requirements, where background details must be dampened while foreground details require high frequencies [S3]. Space-covering volume sampling was proposed by Kraus to extend pre-integrated volume rendering to multidimensional transfer functions, improving accuracy over piecewise linear approximations [S4].
